en.title: Theatre Arts: the whole course
en.short: What Theatre Arts covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Theatre Arts is the study and practice of live performance. It examines how plays and other performance events are written, interpreted, designed, performed, directed, produced and received by audiences. It joins practical work, such as acting, voice, movement, design and stage management, with historical, theoretical and critical study. Drama usually refers to the written text and its structure. Theatre usually refers to the event: performers, space, audience and production. The two are connected but not identical. Theatre Arts also studies ritual, festival, community performance, film and media where these relate to performance. Graduates work in theatre, film, television, radio, education, community development, arts administration and research. The subject asks what performance means, how it is made, and what it does in society.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text: Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a university B.A. Theatre Arts commonly takes four years, with foundation courses first, practical and specialist courses later, and a final project. Some polytechnics offer ND and HND programmes in theatre or performing arts, each usually two years where offered, with attachment between them. The National Universities Commission regulates university programmes and the National Board for Technical Education regulates polytechnic programmes, but institutions still differ. In the United Kingdom, a B.A. (Hons) is commonly three years, sometimes four with a placement or year abroad. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree commonly takes four years and may be a B.A. or a B.F.A. Postgraduate awards include M.A., M.F.A. and Ph.D.; titles, lengths and entry requirements vary. Confirm accreditation, course titles and graduation requirements with your department.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Most courses begin with definitions and elements: what theatre is, dramatic structure, genre, and the roles of audience and performer. You then study world theatre history from Greece to the Renaissance, and from neoclassicism to modern realism. African drama and theatre history follows, including traditional forms, colonial encounters and modern practice, then Nigerian traditions and the modern stage. Script analysis, voice and speech, and movement and the body give you tools for practical work.

The core years build on this. Acting fundamentals and character building lead into improvisation and devised theatre. Directing, stagecraft and design, lighting and sound, stage management, costume and make-up, and theatre spaces show how a production is organised. Dramatic theory and criticism, theatre in education and community theatre, popular theatre and audience studies, playwriting, and theatre practice in Nigeria and Africa today connect practice to context. Ethics and professional practice and research methods prepare you for independent work.

At master’s level, advanced dramatic and performance theory, performance studies, dissertation methods, and intercultural and applied theatre extend the field. Teaching order varies, but the pattern usually moves from understanding, to making, to reflecting and researching.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read plays as scripts for performance, not only as literature. Identify the given circumstances, conflict, characters, structure and intended audience. Say the lines aloud and time them. Watch live or recorded productions and compare choices of acting, design and direction.

Keep a working notebook. Record exercises in voice, movement and improvisation, and note what improved and what failed. Learn terms by using them in rehearsal and in writing. Work in groups, because theatre is collaborative, but keep your own record of your contribution.

For history and theory, learn names, periods, main ideas and one criticism. Always name the country and period. Practices differ, and theatre changes. Use your library and official theatre archives, and cite every source. Check safety rules for rehearsal and performance spaces.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is to think Theatre Arts means acting only. Most of the work is making, organising, writing about and understanding performance. Another is to treat drama and theatre as the same thing, or to study a play without imagining it on stage.

Students also memorise dates without understanding why a period mattered, generalise from one country’s theatre to all theatre, and ignore the audience. In practice, common faults are not learning lines, overacting, ignoring rehearsal safety, and missing deadlines. In writing, they plagiarise, describe a performance without evidence, or use theory without explaining it. Check your handbook and ask your lecturer when a rule or deadline is unclear.

keyPoints: Theatre Arts studies both dramatic texts and live performance events.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Practical work and written study support each other.
Learn theatre history and theory with the country and period attached.
Collaboration is central to theatre, but keep a record of your own contribution.
Name the country when discussing theatre practice, training or rules.

en.title: What Is Theatre? Live Performance and Its Basic Terms
en.short: Theatre as live performance before an audience, and the terms play, script, role, stage and auditorium.

sections.heading: Theatre and drama
sections.text:
Theatre is live performance before an audience. Performers share the same time and place as the people watching, and the event happens once, even if it is repeated on other nights. Drama is the written composition: characters, dialogue and structure, which can be read alone. A drama can exist on the page; theatre needs performance.

Usage varies, and many writers use the two words loosely, but the distinction is useful. It keeps attention on the fact that theatre is an event, not only a text.

sections.heading: Theatre and other performance
sections.text:
Performance is the wider term: any activity set apart and done for watchers, including dance, music, sport and ceremony. Theatre is a kind of performance in which performers represent action, usually through characters and a story.

Ritual is repeated symbolic action, often religious, valued for what it is believed to achieve rather than for entertainment. Theatre and ritual share costumes, music and masks, and scholars argue about how firmly to separate them, but ritual aims at efficacy, bringing about a result, and theatre at showing.

sections.heading: Basic terms
sections.text:
A play is a dramatic work written for performance. The script is its written text, with dialogue and stage directions. A role is the part an actor takes. Performance is the event of playing the work before people.

The audience is the group watching, whose presence and responses shape the event. The auditorium is where the audience sits. The stage is the area where performers act.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text:
A made-up case: a student group in Jos rehearses a published play for three weeks and performs it in a school hall on a Friday evening. The script is the text they worked from; each actor holds a role; the Friday event is the performance; the pupils and parents watching are the audience; the hall is the auditorium; the raised platform is the stage.

If the group only read the play aloud in class, they studied drama, not theatre.

keyPoints: Theatre is live performance before an audience; drama is the written composition.
Performance is the broader term covering dance, music, sport and ceremony; theatre is one kind of it.
Ritual is repeated symbolic action aimed at efficacy, and it is not the same as theatre even where they share features.
A play is a dramatic work, and the script is its written text.
A role is the part an actor takes, and performance is the event itself.
The audience watches and shapes the event, the auditorium seats them, and the stage is where performers act.

en.title: Elements of Drama and Dramatic Structure
en.short: Aristotle’s six elements, theme and dialogue, and the five-part dramatic structure with acts and scenes.

sections.heading: Aristotle’s elements
sections.text: Aristotle’s Poetics names six elements of tragedy: plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle. Plot (mythos) is the arrangement of events. Character (ethos) is moral quality revealed by the agents. Thought (dianoia) is the reasoning expressed. Diction (lexis) is verbal expression, mainly dialogue. Song (melos) is the musical element. Spectacle (opsis) is visual production, including set and costume. Aristotle ranks plot highest and spectacle lowest, because structure carries meaning.

sections.heading: Theme and dialogue
sections.text: Theme is the central idea or question a play explores, such as justice or loyalty. It is not one of Aristotle’s six elements; it is inferred from the whole action. Dialogue is spoken exchange between characters. It advances plot, reveals character, carries thought and creates rhythm. Spectacle and song support drama but cannot replace action: a loud set may entertain, yet the play still needs conflict and choice.

sections.heading: Dramatic structure
sections.text: Dramatic structure is the order in which conflict unfolds. Exposition gives background and initial situation. Rising action adds complications. The climax is the turning point, the moment of greatest tension or decisive choice. Falling action shows consequences. The denouement, French for untying, resolves what remains. In a play about a land dispute, exposition shows two families claiming one field; rising action brings witnesses and letters; the climax is the discovery that a deed was altered; falling action shows reactions; the denouement shows a new agreement or lasting grief. Many plays vary this pattern or leave endings open.

sections.heading: Acts and scenes
sections.text: Acts are major divisions of a play; scenes are smaller units within them. Acts often mark changes of time, place or interval; scenes often begin with an entrance or end with an exit. The number varies by period and country: five-act conventions are common in some European drama, while three-act, two-act and one-act plays are common in modern theatre. Follow the divisions printed in the play text.

keyPoints: Aristotle’s Poetics names six elements: plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle.
Plot is the arrangement of events, and Aristotle ranks it above spectacle.
Theme is the central idea, inferred from the whole play rather than one of Aristotle’s six elements.
Dialogue advances plot, reveals character and carries thought.
The five-part structure is exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and denouement.
Acts are major divisions and scenes are smaller units; their number varies by play and period.

en.title: Dramatic Genres: Tragedy, Comedy and Beyond
en.short: Tragedy, comedy, tragicomedy, melodrama, farce and satire: tone, structure, ending, staging and response.

sections.heading: Tragedy and comedy
sections.text: Genre is a category of play, though real plays mix categories. Tragedy treats serious action and suffering. Its structure links cause to consequence and moves towards downfall; it ends in loss or death. Aristotle connected tragedy with pity, fear and catharsis, commonly explained as release of those feelings. Comedy treats folly with humour. It usually moves from confusion or conflict to reconciliation, often marriage, and ends in renewal. Tragedy’s tone is grave; comedy’s is playful. Acting in tragedy favours controlled voice and sustained tension; comedy needs timing and openness to the audience.

sections.heading: Mixed and heightened forms
sections.text: Tragicomedy mixes serious and comic material. Its structure may turn from threat to laughter, or end without full resolution; the tone shifts, and audiences feel relief mixed with unease. Melodrama heightens emotion and makes good and evil clear. Plot and spectacle dominate character, and the ending is often moral or happy. Farce is fast comedy built on improbable situations, physical action and plot twists; it ends with order restored. Satire uses humour and irony to criticise folly or vice. It is often a mode within comedy rather than a separate genre, and it aims at thought as well as laughter.

sections.heading: Staging and response
sections.text: Each genre shapes staging. Tragedy often uses scale, shadow and strong vertical lines; comedy uses bright colour, flexible space and practical doors. Melodrama calls for spectacle and clear visual signals of virtue and villainy; farce needs precise doors and props for timed entrances. Acting changes too: melodrama uses broad gesture, farce exact physical timing, satire underplayed irony. Audience response follows: tragedy may produce awe and pity, comedy shared laughter, tragicomedy unease, melodrama tears or cheers, farce helpless laughter, satire discomfort and reflection. A simple case: Ada hides a debt from her brother Emeka. As tragedy, the secret destroys them; as comedy, it ends in reconciliation; as satire, it mocks the lender. Genre is a tool, not a fixed box.

keyPoints: Tragedy treats serious suffering and moves towards downfall, often ending in loss or death.
Comedy moves from confusion to reconciliation and usually ends in renewal.
Tragicomedy mixes serious and comic tones and may end without full resolution.
Melodrama heightens emotion and makes moral conflict clear; farce uses improbable situations and physical timing.
Satire uses humour and irony to criticise folly or vice and is often a mode within comedy.
Genre shapes acting, design and audience response, but plays often mix genres.

en.title: World Theatre History I: Greece to the Renaissance
en.short: Greek ritual and Dionysus, Roman comedy, medieval mystery and morality plays, Japanese forms and the Renaissance.

sections.heading: Greek festivals
sections.text:
Greek theatre grew from ritual honouring Dionysus, god of wine. At the City Dionysia in Athens, citizens watched contests of dithyrambs (choral hymns), tragedies and comedies. A dithyramb is a sung, danced narrative. The festival was both worship and civic competition.

In the fifth century BCE, three tragic playwrights each presented a tetralogy: three tragedies and a satyr play, a short comic piece. Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides wrote tragedies; Aristophanes wrote comedies. Actors wore masks in an open-air theatre with a chorus.

sections.heading: Roman theatre
sections.text:
Roman theatre adapted Greek forms. Plautus and Terence wrote comedies with stock characters, fixed types such as the bragging soldier. Seneca wrote rhetorical tragedies that later influenced Renaissance writers.

Roman theatres were free-standing stone buildings, unlike Greek hillside theatres. Pantomime, a silent danced performance, was also popular, but literary drama is the main legacy.

sections.heading: Medieval Europe
sections.text:
After Rome, the Church opposed pagan theatre, but drama returned in liturgical ceremonies. Mystery plays dramatised Bible stories; miracle plays told of saints.

In England, craft guilds performed mystery cycles at the feast of Corpus Christi. Morality plays such as Everyman used allegorical characters to teach Christian conduct. These were staged on wagons or in marketplaces.

sections.heading: Japan and Renaissance
sections.text:
Japanese theatre developed separately. Noh, refined by Zeami in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, combines masks, dance, chant and slow movement. Kabuki, a popular dance-drama, and Bunraku, the puppet theatre, emerged in the seventeenth century.

In Europe, the Renaissance revived classical learning. Commedia dell’arte, Italian improvised comedy with stock masks, flourished from the sixteenth century. Shakespeare wrote for the Globe in London; Lope de Vega and Calderón led Spanish Golden Age theatre. These forms shaped later theatre in Europe.

keyPoints: Greek theatre began in festivals of Dionysus, especially the City Dionysia in Athens.
Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides wrote Greek tragedy; Aristophanes wrote comedy.
Roman comedy is represented by Plautus and Terence; Seneca wrote tragedy.
Medieval mystery plays dramatised Bible stories, and morality plays taught conduct through allegory.
Noh, Kabuki and Bunraku are major Japanese theatre forms.
Renaissance theatre includes commedia dell’arte, Shakespeare and the Spanish Golden Age.

en.title: World Theatre History II: Neoclassicism to Modern Realism
en.short: French neoclassicism, Restoration comedy, melodrama, the well-made play, realism and naturalism, and the realist stage.

sections.heading: French rules
sections.text:
French neoclassicism was a seventeenth-century movement that applied rules drawn from Aristotle and Horace. Its main rules were the three unities: unity of action (one main plot), unity of time (usually one day) and unity of place (one setting).

It also demanded verisimilitude, meaning events must seem probable, and decorum, meaning language and behaviour must suit rank. Tragedy and comedy stayed separate. Corneille, Racine and Molière wrote within or against these rules, which aimed to make drama clear and moral.

sections.heading: Restoration comedy
sections.text:
English Restoration comedy flourished after 1660, when the monarchy returned and London theatres reopened. It is often called comedy of manners: witty plays about love, money and reputation among the upper classes.

Plots turn on intrigue, disguise and sexual attraction, and the language is polished and ironic. Playwrights include Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve and Farquhar. Actresses appeared on the English public stage in this period, unlike the earlier all-male theatre.

sections.heading: Melodrama to realism
sections.text:
Melodrama rose in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It used music, spectacle, stock characters and clear moral conflict: innocent virtue suffers, then is rescued. It appealed to popular audiences.

The well-made play, developed by Eugène Scribe and later Victorien Sardou, had a tight plot with a secret, complications, a climax and a neat denouement, the final resolution of the plot. Realism argued for truthful observation of ordinary life. Naturalism added that heredity and environment determine behaviour; Émile Zola was a leading theorist.

sections.heading: Realist stage
sections.text:
The realist stage of the late nineteenth century put ordinary people and social problems on stage. Henrik Ibsen’s A Doll’s House (1879) ends with Nora leaving her husband, which shocked audiences.

August Strindberg’s Miss Julie (1888) examines class and sexual conflict. Anton Chekhov’s The Seagull (1896) and The Cherry Orchard (1904) use understatement and ensemble scenes to show change in provincial life. These writers wanted believable dialogue, psychological detail and visible social pressures.

keyPoints: French neoclassicism enforced the three unities, verisimilitude and decorum, and kept tragedy and comedy separate.
English Restoration comedy is comedy of manners, marked by wit, intrigue and upper-class settings.
Melodrama used music, spectacle and clear moral conflict to appeal to popular audiences.
The well-made play built a tight plot around a secret, complications and a neat denouement.
Realism sought truthful observation of ordinary life, while naturalism stressed heredity and environment.
Ibsen, Strindberg and Chekhov made believable dialogue and social pressure central to the realist stage.

en.title: African Drama and Theatre: Traditional Forms to Modern Practice
en.short: African performance forms, written drama, Yoruba travelling theatre, Soyinka and Ngugi.

sections.heading: Traditional forms
sections.text: Traditional African performance is older than written African drama. Masquerade is performance in which a masked figure represents a spirit, ancestor or community character; the mask hides the wearer and changes the body. Storytelling uses a narrator, call and response, song, gesture and audience participation. Ritual drama shapes action around worship, initiation or healing. Festival theatre gathers these forms in public celebration, often tied to a calendar. Forms vary by community, so avoid treating one as typical of the continent.

sections.heading: Written drama
sections.text: Written African drama grew in the twentieth century through schools, churches, newspapers and universities. Early plays appeared in English, French, Portuguese and African languages. Writers borrowed story, song and masquerade rather than replacing oral forms. Language became central. Ngugi wa Thiong’o, a Kenyan novelist and playwright, argued in Decolonising the Mind (1986) that African writers should create in African languages. Others chose English or French to reach wider audiences. Both raise questions of audience, translation and colonial history.

sections.heading: Yoruba travelling theatre
sections.text: The Yoruba travelling theatre of south-west Nigeria developed from the 1940s. Troupes toured towns and performed in Yoruba, mixing music, dance, mime, comedy and topical satire. Hubert Ogunde is often called a pioneer; Kola Ogunmola and Duro Ladipo led famous companies. Troupes played in halls, open spaces and later on television. Their style influenced written drama and modern Nigerian theatre. It shows how oral performance can become professional commercial theatre without losing its language and audience.

sections.heading: Soyinka and Ngugi
sections.text: Wole Soyinka, a Nigerian playwright, combines Yoruba ritual, myth, satire and complex language. His plays include A Dance of the Forests (1960) and Death and the King’s Horseman (1975). In 1986 he became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Ngugi wa Thiong’o wrote I Will Marry When I Want (1977) in Gikuyu with Ngugi wa Mirii. Their work shows two paths: international literary drama and committed African-language theatre.

keyPoints: African performance includes masquerade, storytelling, ritual drama and festival, and forms vary by community.
Written African drama developed in the twentieth century and borrowed from oral performance.
The language debate asks whether to write in English, French or African languages.
The Yoruba travelling theatre made professional popular theatre in Yoruba from the 1940s.
Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986; Ngugi wa Thiong’o wrote plays in Gikuyu.

en.title: Nigerian Theatre Traditions and the Modern Stage
en.short: Yoruba Alarinjo, Igbo mmanwu, Hausa koroso, Kambari forms, school drama, Ibadan and Ife schools, National Troupe.

sections.heading: Performance traditions
sections.text: Nigerian performance traditions are community-based: music, dance, costume and audience response are part of the event. Yoruba Alarinjo is a travelling masquerade theatre of masked performers, drumming, dance and satire; popular Yoruba theatre later drew on Apala, a Yoruba popular music style, and other music. Igbo mmanwu is a masquerade tradition in which masked figures embody spirits and comment on community life. Hausa koroso is an acrobatic dance display with drumming and energetic movement. Kambari communities keep masquerade and dance forms tied to festivals and rites. These are living practices, not relics.

sections.heading: School drama
sections.text: School drama means plays staged by schools, colleges and teacher-training institutions, often for speech days, festivals or literary societies. In Nigeria it grew under mission and colonial education, then expanded after independence. Pupils performed English classics and later Nigerian plays, and school festivals fed audiences into the modern stage. A first-year class can test this by staging a short Alarinjo-style prologue: one drummer, two masked actors and a chorus. The class must keep the story clear and the community comment respectful.

sections.heading: Ibadan and Ife
sections.text: The University of Ibadan developed an academic drama programme and a theatre company. The Ibadan school is associated with literary playwriting and script-centred production. The University of Ife, now Obafemi Awolowo University, built a dramatic arts programme known for total theatre: drama combined with music, dance and indigenous performance. The Ife school encouraged ensemble work and African forms. Both schools trained actors, directors, designers and scholars, and their debate shaped modern Nigerian theatre.

sections.heading: National Troupe
sections.text: The National Troupe of Nigeria is a federal performing company. It performs at national events and abroad, and it aims to support national unity and cultural diplomacy. For a student, the lesson is that modern Nigerian theatre has three linked layers: community traditions, school and university training, and state-supported companies. Each layer borrows from the others, and none replaces the rest.

keyPoints: Alarinjo is a Yoruba travelling masquerade theatre using masks, music, dance and satire.
Igbo mmanwu is a masquerade tradition in which masked figures embody spirits and comment on community life.
Hausa koroso is an acrobatic dance display, and Kambari communities keep masquerade and dance forms.
School drama grew through schools and colleges and fed audiences into modern Nigerian theatre.
The University of Ibadan school stressed literary drama, while the University of Ife (now OAU) school stressed total theatre.
The National Troupe of Nigeria presents Nigerian dance, music and drama for national unity and cultural diplomacy.

en.title: Reading and Analysing a Play Script
en.short: Close reading for scene breakdown, beats, objectives, given circumstances, subtext and stage directions.

sections.heading: Break the script down
sections.text:
Read the whole play once for the story, then again with a pencil. A scene breakdown lists each scene, who enters and exits, the place and time, and the key event. Ask what changes by the end of the scene. If nothing changes, the unit may belong to a larger scene.

Given circumstances are the facts the script supplies about the world and the character: period, place, social rules, age, health, money, family and past. In an invented scene, a market trader, Adaeze, owes a creditor and hides a letter when her brother arrives. Her debt and his sudden visit shape every choice she makes.

sections.heading: Beats and objectives
sections.text:
A beat is the smallest unit of action in which a character pursues one objective until something changes. An objective is what the character wants in that beat, stated as an active verb: to persuade, to hide, to comfort. Subtext is the meaning beneath the words, often a gap between words and behaviour.

In the invented scene, Adaeze says, 'You are welcome.' Her objective may be to get her brother out before the creditor comes. The subtext is fear. The actor plays the objective, not the label 'fear'. Write a beat chart: scene, beat, objective, obstacle, action. This turns the script into actable choices.

sections.heading: Stage directions and plan
sections.text:
Stage directions are the playwright’s written instructions: setting, entrances, exits, pauses, tone or movement. They may be in italics or brackets. Treat them as evidence. Ask whether a direction is essential to the action or only a suggestion. Playwrights differ: some give detailed directions, others few.

A performance plan turns analysis into work. It can include a scene list, beat chart, blocking (planned movement), props, costume, cues and rehearsal questions. For the invented scene: Scene 2, beat 1, objective 'to hide the letter', blocking 'stand between brother and table', prop 'letter', cue 'brother’s knock'. Check every plan line against the script, and revise in rehearsal.

keyPoints: A scene breakdown records scenes, entrances and exits, place, time and the key change.
Given circumstances are the facts the script gives about the world and character.
A beat is a unit of action with one objective; state objectives as active verbs.
Subtext is meaning beneath the words, often a gap between speech and behaviour.
Stage directions are evidence and clues, not always rigid commands.
A performance plan combines scene list, beat chart, blocking, props and cues, checked against the script.

en.title: Voice and Speech for the Actor
en.short: Breath support, resonance, articulation, projection, pace, pause, English and Nigerian diction, daily warm-ups.

sections.heading: Breath and support
sections.text: Breath support means controlling the outward flow of air with the muscles of the lower ribs and abdomen, not grabbing at the throat. Stand tall, release the jaw and shoulders, and breathe low into the back and sides of the ribs. On a soft “sss”, keep the stream steady for a slow count. A simple check: inhale for 4 counts, hiss for 8, then 12, without raising the shoulders. Stop before tension. Support gives the voice enough air for long phrases and protects it from strain.

sections.heading: Resonance and projection
sections.text: Resonance is the way air in the throat, mouth and nasal spaces makes the voice fuller. Hum gently, feel vibration in the lips, face and chest, then open to “ma, me, mi, mo, mu”. Projection is not shouting; it is clear, supported speech aimed at the back row. Imagine speaking to a person at the back wall, keep the neck free, and let consonants carry. If the voice hurts or fades, return to breath and resonance.

sections.heading: Articulation and diction
sections.text: Articulation is the precise movement of tongue, lips, jaw and soft palate that shapes sounds. Diction is clear and acceptable pronunciation in performance. In English, distinguish final consonants and avoid swallowing endings: “acted”, not “acte”. Vowel length matters: “ship” and “sheep” differ. Many Nigerian languages, including Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa, use tone to change meaning. Respect tone, vowel length and nasal sounds. Yoruba “ọ” and “o”, Igbo “ị” and “i”, and Hausa sounds such as ɓ, ɗ and ƙ are not interchangeable with English sounds. Ask a native-speaker coach. Do not imitate a foreign accent unless the role requires it.

sections.heading: Pace, pause, warm-up
sections.text: Pace is speed of speech; pause is silence used for meaning. Vary pace. Pause before a key word or after a question. Warm-up: shake shoulders; breathe low for 4 counts and hiss for 8; hum five times; say tongue twisters slowly, then faster; read a short speech aloud, marking breaths and pauses. Never force a tired voice.

keyPoints: Breath support controls airflow with the lower ribs and abdomen, not the throat.
Resonance makes the voice fuller; projection is supported speech aimed at the back row, not shouting.
Articulation shapes sounds, while diction is clear and appropriate pronunciation.
Many Nigerian languages use tone, vowel length and sounds absent from English, so respect them.
Vary pace and use pauses to carry meaning on stage.
A short daily warm-up protects the voice and improves clarity.

en.title: Movement and the Actor’s Body
en.short: Posture, alignment, relaxation, stage zones and levels, Laban efforts, mime and physical theatre.

sections.heading: Posture and relaxation
sections.text:
Posture is how the body holds itself against gravity. Good alignment stacks the head over the pelvis and the weight over the feet, knees soft rather than locked. It is not stiffness: it lets breath move and the spine lengthen.

Relaxation means releasing tension the work does not need, in the jaw, shoulders and neck. It is not going limp. A short warm-up of spine, hips and ankles prevents strain.

sections.heading: Levels and stage zones
sections.text:
Spatial awareness starts with the kinesphere, the space the limbs reach without moving the feet, and grows to fill the whole stage.

Stage areas are named from the actor’s view facing the audience. Upstage is away from the audience; downstage is nearest. A common grid divides the floor into nine zones, three rows of left, centre and right. Some people use house left and right, named from the audience’s view, so agree on terms first.

Levels are high (standing), middle (sitting or kneeling) and low (lying). Changing level changes status and focus.

sections.heading: Laban’s effort factors
sections.text:
Rudolf Laban described movement through four effort factors: weight (strong or light), time (quick or sustained), space (direct or indirect) and flow (bound or free). Combining weight, time and space gives eight effort actions, among them press (strong, sustained, direct), punch (strong, quick, direct), glide (light, sustained, direct) and float (light, sustained, indirect).

Case: Ada plays a servant carrying a heavy pot. Strong, sustained, direct movement gives press, and a low level with a slow, bound walk shows the load. Played light and quick, the same entrance reads as a dancer.

sections.heading: Mime and physical theatre
sections.text: Mime tells a story through the body alone. Étienne Decroux developed corporeal mime; his student Marcel Marceau made the white-faced mime famous. Jacques Lecoq taught physical theatre through neutral mask and play. Such training builds precision, weight and economy, and helps an actor decide how a character stands, walks and rests.

keyPoints: Alignment stacks head, pelvis and feet so the body can breathe and move without strain.
Relaxation is the release of unnecessary tension, not collapse.
Stage areas are named from the actor’s view facing the audience: upstage is away from them, downstage nearest.
Levels (high, middle, low) and the nine zones give variety and show status and focus.
Laban’s four effort factors are weight, time, space and flow; combining weight, time and space gives eight effort actions such as press, punch, glide and float.
Mime and physical theatre train economy and precision, and help build a character’s body.

en.title: Building a Character: Stanislavski, Method and Ensemble
en.short: Stanislavski’s system, method acting, African ensemble practice and rehearsal into behaviour.

sections.heading: Stanislavski’s system
sections.text: Stanislavski’s system is a set of training ideas, not fixed rules. Given circumstances are the facts and conditions of the play: time, place, relationships and past events. An objective is what the character wants in a unit of action, phrased as a verb such as to persuade or to protect. The super-objective is the character’s whole aim through the play. Actions are what the actor does to pursue an objective. Beats are small units where the objective or tactic changes. Emotional memory means recalling a personal experience to stir feeling. Stanislavski used it early but later stressed imagination and physical action, and warned against self-indulgence.

sections.heading: Method and ensemble
sections.text: Method acting is a broad American development from Stanislavski. Lee Strasberg’s Method uses affective memory and relaxation. Stella Adler stressed given circumstances and imagination. Sanford Meisner trained attention on the partner. So method is not one technique. Many African performance traditions work through ensemble and improvisation: group-devised scenes, call-and-response, music, dance and audience feedback. Yoruba travelling theatre and Ghanaian concert party are examples, but practices vary widely and should not be treated as one system.

sections.heading: Rehearsal into behaviour
sections.text: Rehearsal turns analysis into behaviour. The actor reads the scene, names circumstances and objectives, breaks it into beats, chooses playable actions, then tests them in improvisation and repetition. Example: Ngozi plays a sister hiding a debt. Her super-objective is to keep the family together. In one beat her objective is to calm her brother; her action is to offer him food and change the subject. When that fails, she changes tactic. The audience should see the behaviour, not the analysis.

keyPoints: Given circumstances are the play’s facts and conditions, such as time, place and relationships.
An objective is a want expressed as a playable verb, and the super-objective is the character’s whole aim.
Beats are units in which the objective or tactic changes.
Emotional memory recalls personal feeling, but Stanislavski later stressed imagination and physical action.
Method acting is not one technique: Strasberg, Adler and Meisner differ.
Rehearsal tests objectives through action until behaviour becomes spontaneous.

en.title: Improvisation and Devised Theatre
en.short: Improvisation games, status work, devising methods, shaping scenes and crediting collective authorship.

sections.heading: Improvisation games
sections.text: Improvisation is acting without a fixed script. Viola Spolin’s theatre games (1963) use simple rules: who, what, where; give and take; no blocking. Keith Johnstone’s Impro (1979) stresses accepting offers. The core rule is "yes, and": accept what a partner gives and add to it. Games train listening, quick choices and ensemble trust. They are not yet performance.

sections.heading: Status work
sections.text: Status is the relative power between people in a scene, not social rank. Keith Johnstone showed that high-status behaviour (stillness, holding gaze, slow speech) and low-status behaviour (fidgeting, looking away, agreeing) can be played. In a paired exercise, one player starts high and the other low; then they swap without saying so. The audience sees the shift. Status transactions make ordinary words dramatic.

sections.heading: Devising methods
sections.text: Devised theatre is created by a company, not from a finished script. Starting points include an image, object, theme, news story or movement score. Methods include improvisation, writing in character, Viewpoints (a vocabulary of time and space developed by Mary Overlie and adapted by Anne Bogart and Tina Landau), and composing scenes from repeated actions. The director acts as editor and outside eye; a dramaturg helps research and structure. Document notes, recordings and scripts. Suppose a Lagos ensemble, with director Amaka and actors Tunde and Chidi, starts with a market photograph: one actor improvises a trader, another a customer, and they record the scene.

sections.heading: Shaping and crediting
sections.text: A company shapes raw material by selecting the strongest scenes, ordering them, and cutting repetition. Rehearse transitions and test the whole piece before an audience. Collective authorship means crediting everyone who contributed text, movement or staging. Put a written agreement in place: who owns the work, how royalties are split, and how future productions credit the company. Copyright rules differ by country, so check the national law. A simple credit might read "devised by the company", with individual roles listed.

keyPoints: Improvisation trains listening and acceptance through games and the "yes, and" rule.
Status is relative power in a scene, shown through behaviour, not social rank.
Devised theatre starts from stimuli and uses improvisation, writing and composition.
A director or outside eye shapes raw scenes into a coherent piece.
Collective authorship requires written agreements on ownership, royalties and credit.
Check national copyright law because credit and rights rules differ by country.

en.title: Directing for the Theatre
en.short: The director’s work: script analysis, concept, casting, rehearsal, blocking, design and notes.

sections.heading: Reading and concept
sections.text: The director begins with script analysis: read the play many times to find its action, its world and its central question. The director’s analysis asks what the play wants from an audience. From this comes the concept, the production’s guiding interpretation: period, style, visual world and tone. A concept must serve the play, not decorate it. The director then agrees practical limits with producers: budget, venue, dates and audience.

sections.heading: Casting and rehearsal
sections.text: Casting matches actors to roles through auditions and callbacks; the director considers suitability, chemistry and availability. Callbacks are second auditions with selected actors. A rehearsal plan sets dates, scenes, deadlines and runs. Early rehearsals explore meaning and relationships; later ones fix blocking, the planned movement and stage positions. The director keeps a prompt copy, the master script with cues, and works with stage management.

sections.heading: Design and blocking
sections.text: The director meets designers of set, costume, lighting and sound to agree a shared visual and sound world. Blocking should reveal status, relationships and story, not merely fill space. In a small case, a director in Ibadan staging a family dispute might place the father upstage behind a table and the daughter downstage, so distance shows power. Upstage is away from the audience; downstage is nearer. The director checks sightlines, the audience’s clear lines of view, and safe spacing.

sections.heading: Notes and responsibility
sections.text: Notes are short, specific comments after rehearsal or performance. Good notes name the moment, the effect and a workable adjustment, and are given privately where possible. Written notes should be few enough to act on. Tempo is speed; rhythm is the pattern of pauses, stresses and changes. The director shapes both in long runs, not by rushing lines. Finally, the director accepts responsibility for the finished production: coherence, safety, ethics and the audience’s experience.

keyPoints: A director interprets the script through a concept that serves the play.
Casting and rehearsal planning turn interpretation into workable stage action.
Blocking uses stage position to show relationships, status and story.
Designers and director agree a shared visual and sound world.
Notes should be specific, timely and workable.
The director carries final responsibility for coherence, safety and the audience’s experience.

en.title: Stagecraft and Theatrical Design
en.short: Set, costume, make-up and props design, and the process from research to model and production meeting.

sections.heading: The design areas
sections.text:
Stagecraft is the practical craft of putting a performance on a stage. Scenery, or the set, is the physical world the actors move in. The set designer, often called the scenographer, decides its shape, levels and materials. The costume designer plans what each character wears. The make-up designer plans face, hair and wigs. The props manager supplies properties: the objects actors carry and handle, such as cups, letters or weapons.

Job titles and duties differ between countries, companies and whether the work is commercial or amateur. In small productions one person may do all of these jobs.

sections.heading: Design and meaning
sections.text:
Design is not decoration added after the acting is settled. It tells the audience where and when the action happens, what kind of people these are, and what the play is about. Colour, texture, height and emptiness all carry mood before anyone speaks.

A small case: a student production of a play about a family losing its land. Grey bare platforms and one good chair could suggest loss and memory. A fully furnished, comfortable room would say the opposite. The designer reads the script for its theme, then chooses images that support it.

sections.heading: The design process
sections.text:
The work usually follows a sequence. Read the script closely, then research the period, place and social detail. Next come rough sketches, which are tested in a scale model, a small three-dimensional mock-up often built at 1:25 or 1:50, and in drawings. A ground plan shows the set from above, so the director can plan movement. Elevations show the set’s faces straight on, such as the front the audience sees. A rendering is a coloured picture of the finished look.

The designer brings all of this to the production meeting with the director, stage manager and technical staff. There they agree budget, materials, build time and safety. Designs keep changing through rehearsals, and the final check comes at the technical and dress rehearsals.

keyPoints: Stagecraft includes scenery, costume, make-up and props, each with its own specialist.
Design carries meaning: place, period, character and theme.
Research and script reading come before any drawing.
A scale model and a ground plan let the whole team see the design before it is built.
The production meeting settles budget, materials, build time and safety.
Designs are revised through rehearsals up to the technical and dress rehearsals.

en.title: Lighting and Sound for Performance
en.short: Covers stage lighting, colour, focus, cues, sound design, reinforcement and safety.

sections.heading: Lighting functions and instruments
sections.text:
Stage lighting makes actors visible, shapes mood and time, directs focus and supports the story. A lantern is a fixture.

The fresnel gives a soft-edged beam and uses barn doors to cut spill. The profile gives a hard edge and uses shutters or a gobo, a template, to shape light. A PAR or LED wash gives a broad, even field. A dimmer controls lamp intensity; LED fixtures may dim electronically. A console stores and replays states.

sections.heading: Colour, angle and focus
sections.text:
Colour in light mixes additively: red, green and blue light make white. A gel is a coloured filter in front of a lantern; it subtracts colours from white light. A blue gel looks different under a warm tungsten lamp and a cool LED. Colour temperature describes warmth or coolness, often in kelvin.

Angles matter: front light shows the face but flattens; side light models form; back light separates actor from background; top light casts shadows. Focus means aiming the lantern, setting beam size and sharpness, and cutting unwanted light. For a night scene, use low blue side light and dim back light, not a bright white front wash.

sections.heading: Cues, sound and safety
sections.text:
A lighting cue is a recorded change: number, trigger, action and time. Example: LX 12, on the line “I am leaving”, bring the stage-left special, a lantern set for one small area, to 60 per cent over 3 seconds. A sound cue works the same way: SQ 4, on the door slam, play the recorded slam at 80 per cent and fade after 2 seconds. Sound design plans music, effects, ambience and voices.

Sound reinforcement amplifies live sound: a microphone feeds a mixing console, which balances levels and sends them to speakers. The designer sets gain, the input level, for a clean signal and balanced tone. Feedback (howl) happens when a microphone picks up sound from the speakers; careful placement and tone control limit it. Equipment and safety rules differ by venue and country: rigging, electrical work, heat, noise, cable routes must follow the venue’s risk assessment and local regulations. Never rig or rewire unless trained and authorised.

keyPoints: Lighting makes actors visible, shapes mood and focus, and supports the story.
A fresnel gives a soft beam; a profile gives a hard edge and can use shutters or a gobo.
Light colour mixes additively, and a gel subtracts colour from white light.
Focus means aiming, sizing and shaping each lantern’s beam.
A cue needs a number, trigger, action and timing; sound cues follow the same logic.
Sound reinforcement balances live voices and playback through a console and speakers, and all rigging and electrical work must follow local and venue safety rules.

en.title: Stage Management and Production Organisation
en.short: Stage manager roles, prompt book, schedules, paperwork, budgets and calling cues.

sections.heading: The stage management team
sections.text: The stage management team organises rehearsals and performances. The stage manager leads the team, keeps communication between director, designers, cast and crew, and is responsible for the safe and orderly running of each day. A deputy stage manager, often called the DSM, may be “on the book”: following the script and calling cues. An assistant stage manager, or ASM, often handles props, set pieces and scene changes. Titles and duties vary between countries and companies, and small productions may combine roles.

sections.heading: Prompt book and schedules
sections.text: The prompt book is the stage manager’s master copy. It holds the script, blocking (actors’ movements), cue numbers, lighting and sound plots, props and scene-change lists, contact details and schedules. A rehearsal schedule states which scenes, actors and rooms are needed, and when. Rehearsal reports record what was done, what changed and what is still needed. These documents let a complex production repeat the same result at every performance.

sections.heading: Paperwork and budget
sections.text: Production paperwork includes the contact sheet, daily call, props list, scene-change plot, cue sheets and risk assessments. A production budget lists expected income and expenses. Suppose a small show has expenses of 100,000 units: venue 40,000, set 25,000, costumes 10,000, lighting and sound 15,000, publicity 5,000 and contingency, a reserve for unexpected costs, 5,000. The total is 100,000. If 150 seats are sold at 800 units for each of two performances, income is 150 × 800 × 2 = 240,000. Production meetings track money, time and decisions.

sections.heading: Running the show
sections.text: Running the show means checking the space, set, props and crew before the audience enters. The stage manager or deputy stage manager gives calls such as “half hour” and “five minutes”, then “standby” before a cue and “go” to execute it. Cues are written in the prompt book and called in a fixed order. After the performance, the team notes faults and resets for the next show. Clear communication and a written chain of responsibility keep a company reliable.

keyPoints: The stage manager leads the stage management team and coordinates rehearsals and performances.
The deputy stage manager often follows the prompt book and calls cues, while assistant stage managers handle props and scene changes; titles vary.
The prompt book collects the script, blocking, cues, plots, contacts and schedules.
A rehearsal schedule sets what is rehearsed, by whom, where and when.
Production paperwork and budgets track contacts, props, cues, risks, income and expenses.
For a simple budget, total expenses = sum of expense lines and ticket income = tickets sold × price × performances.

en.title: Costume and Make-up for the Stage
en.short: Costume design, construction, ageing, character make-up and quick-change planning for the stage.

sections.heading: Design from the script
sections.text:
Costume design begins with the script, the director’s concept and the actor’s body. The designer makes a costume plot: a list of every character, scene and change. Each costume must show age, class, occupation, period and mood, and must allow movement, dance or fights.

A student production set in a Lagos market might dress a trader in a faded wrapper and head tie, with a hidden pocket for a phone, because the character must look poor but still move freely.

sections.heading: Construction and ageing
sections.text:
Construction turns the design into a garment that survives rehearsals and performances. Take measurements, make a toile (a test garment in cheap cloth), fit it, then cut the final fabric. Use strong seams, deep hems and washable fabrics.

Ageing, also called breakdown, makes new clothes look old: sandpaper, tea or dye, patches and careful cutting. Keep a spare set of small parts. A costume that cannot be washed or repaired between shows will fail.

sections.heading: Make-up and character
sections.text:
Character make-up changes the face to suit role, age or species. Corrective make-up only balances the face for stage light. Character work uses highlight and shadow: light on a raised area, dark in a hollow. Ageing adds lines, stipple (small dots) and grey in the hair.

Test products on the skin first, and keep brushes clean. Prosthetics, such as false noses, need fixing and a skin test.

sections.heading: Distance, light and quick changes
sections.text:
At distance, the audience reads silhouette (outline), colour value (lightness or darkness) and contrast before fine detail. Avoid tiny patterns and weak colours. Under coloured light, pigments change: a red dress under green light looks dark, and white takes the colour of the gel (the lighting filter). Test costumes and make-up under the actual stage light.

For quick changes, make a change plot with preset positions, dressers (change helpers) and fastenings such as magnets or snaps. Rehearse the change in costume, with timing, and label every piece.

keyPoints: A costume plot lists every character, scene and change, and design starts from the script, concept and actor’s needs.
Build costumes for durability, fit and washing, using a toile and strong fastenings.
Ageing or breakdown makes new costumes look old; character make-up uses highlight and shadow to change the face.
At stage distance, silhouette, colour value and contrast matter more than fine detail.
Coloured light changes how pigments read, so test costume and make-up under the actual stage light.
Plan quick changes with a change plot, preset pieces, dressers and rehearsed fastenings.

en.title: Theatre Spaces and Architecture
en.short: Thrust, proscenium, arena, found and outdoor spaces: sightlines, acoustics, backstage and choice.

sections.heading: Space types
sections.text: Proscenium, thrust, arena, found and outdoor spaces create audience relationships. A proscenium arch frames the stage on one side, hides backstage work and supports illusion, but separates actor and spectator. A thrust stage projects into the auditorium with spectators on three sides, bringing actors close and making entrances visible. An arena stage is surrounded on four sides, so no side is front and scenery must stay low or hang above. A found space is an existing place not built as a theatre, used for performance. An outdoor space is open to weather and daylight. The relationships are frontal, intimate, encircling or shared.

sections.heading: Sightlines and acoustics
sections.text: A sightline is the line from a seat to the stage. Designers check that every seat can see the action; a raked auditorium, with rising rows, improves this. Thrust and arena stages expose actors on several sides, so actors must turn and share focus. Proscenium stages concentrate sightlines but can make side seats feel remote. Acoustics is how sound behaves in a room. Hard surfaces reflect sound and soft surfaces absorb it. Proscenium arches can frame sound, while open thrust and arena stages let voices spread. Outdoor sound escapes, so actors need strong vocal support and may use amplification.

sections.heading: Backstage and choice
sections.text: Backstage layout means the spaces supporting performance. A proscenium theatre has wings, a fly tower for lifting scenery, a crossover passage behind the stage, dressing rooms and a control room. Thrust and arena stages have less wing space, so entrances come through aisles or vomitories, passages through the seating. Found and outdoor spaces need temporary control positions, power, weather cover and safe routes. Choose a space by the script, closeness, technical needs, budget and access. Suppose an Ibadan company stages a play for two actors about market traders. A proscenium may suit hidden costume changes; a thrust may suit direct address; an arena may suit a low budget; a courtyard may suit local meaning but demand good acoustics. Practice varies by country and building.

keyPoints: Proscenium staging is frontal and hides backstage work, while thrust and arena staging bring the audience closer on three or four sides.
Sightlines must be checked from every seat, and raked seating improves views.
Acoustics depends on reflection and absorption; outdoor sound escapes.
Backstage layout includes wings, a fly tower, a crossover passage, dressing rooms and control space, and it changes with the stage form.
Choose a space by script needs, audience closeness, technical support, budget and access.
Found and outdoor spaces can create strong local meaning but need adaptation for safety, sound and weather.

en.title: Dramatic Theory and Theatre Criticism
en.short: Aristotle, neoclassical unities, Brecht and Artaud, and how to review a production fairly.

sections.heading: Aristotle and the unities
sections.text:
Aristotle’s Poetics treats tragedy as an imitation of action that arouses pity and fear and effects catharsis, a purging or clarification of emotion. He ranks plot above character and calls for unity of action: events should form one probable whole. Catharsis is debated: purgation, clarification or both.

Later neoclassical critics added the unities of time, often one day, and place, one setting. These are rules of Italian and French criticism, not Aristotle’s own. They sought verisimilitude, what an audience would accept as probable.

sections.heading: Brecht and Artaud
sections.text:
Brecht’s epic theatre wants audiences to think, not only feel. Narration, episodic scenes, placards and the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) make the familiar strange so spectators judge social conditions. Gestus means a gesture or stage action that shows a social attitude.

Artaud’s theatre of cruelty wants the opposite: to assault the senses through sound, light, gesture and ritual, bypassing psychology and argument. Cruelty here means a metaphysical shock, not literal violence. Both oppose realistic empathy, but for different ends.

sections.heading: Writing the review
sections.text:
A fair review states the production’s aims, then judges it by evidence from the performance. Describe, analyse, evaluate. Say what you saw: a pause, a colour, a blocked entrance. Explain its effect. Compare the result with the director’s apparent intention and the play’s demands. Balance strengths and weaknesses, and name the audience and context. Avoid reviewing the play you expected. A campus Oedipus that uses chorus and drums may fail at clarity but succeed at ritual. Say so, with examples.

Quote briefly from the programme or director’s note only to establish intention, not to excuse weak work. A review is not a plot summary; summarise only what supports your judgement.

keyPoints: Aristotle’s Poetics ranks plot above character and defines tragedy through pity, fear and catharsis.
The neoclassical unities of action, time and place were later rules, not Aristotle’s own.
Brecht’s epic theatre uses alienation and gestus to make spectators judge social conditions.
Artaud’s theatre of cruelty seeks a sensory, ritual shock rather than psychological realism.
A fair review describes evidence from the performance, analyses its effect and evaluates against the production’s aims.
Balance strengths and weaknesses and judge the production, not the play you expected.

en.title: Theatre in Education and Community Theatre
en.short: TIE, Theatre for Development, community practice, workshop design, forum theatre and impact evaluation.

sections.heading: Three practices
sections.text:
Theatre in Education (TIE) is a planned programme in which actor-teachers use drama, role play and discussion to explore a topic with school students, usually linked to the curriculum. It is not just a play performed to them.

Theatre for Development (TfD) is participatory theatre made with a community to examine shared problems and possible actions, often in local languages and forms. Community-based practice means theatre by and with community members rather than professionals performing at them. All three treat the audience as participants, not passive spectators.

sections.heading: Designing workshops
sections.text:
A workshop needs a clear aim, a named group, and a safe space. Plan a warm-up, a main activity, and a closing reflection. Agree ground rules and consent, especially when people will act out personal experiences. The facilitator guides rather than directs.

In a made-up case, facilitator Amina works with traders in a Lagos market on waste disposal. She starts with a name game, then image theatre, where bodies make still pictures of the problem. The group discusses what they see before building a short scene.

sections.heading: Forum theatre
sections.text:
Forum theatre comes from Augusto Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed. A short scene shows an oppression and ends badly.

The joker, a neutral facilitator, invites spect-actors to stop the action and replace a character to test a change. The aim is to rehearse action, not to find one correct answer. It can build confidence and reveal shared problems, but it does not by itself change laws or services.

sections.heading: Evaluating impact
sections.text:
Impact means changes in knowledge, attitudes, skills or actions. Evaluate against the project’s aims, not only attendance. Use mixed methods: short before-and-after questionnaires, focus groups, interviews and observation.

Triangulate, meaning compare more than one source. Seek consent and keep responses anonymous. A single workshop rarely proves long-term change, so report limits honestly. In the market case, follow-up interviews could ask which ideas traders used and what blocked them.

keyPoints: TIE uses actor-teachers and drama to explore curriculum topics with students.
TfD is participatory theatre made with a community to examine problems and test actions.
Community-based practice puts community members at the centre as makers, not just viewers.
Forum theatre uses a joker and spect-actors to stop and change a short scene of oppression.
Workshop design needs a clear aim, consent, safe space, active methods and reflection.
Impact evaluation should use mixed methods and report limits honestly.

en.title: Popular Theatre, Mass Media and the Audience
en.short: Covers popular theatre, Nigerian travelling and stand-up comedy, media reach, audience research and house economics.

sections.heading: Popular and commercial
sections.text: Popular theatre means forms made for a broad, often paying audience, using music, comedy, spectacle and familiar stories. Commercial theatre is produced to earn money, so it watches costs and ticket sales closely. Nigerian travelling theatre troupes toured towns with plays that mixed songs, dance and drama, often in Yoruba. Stand-up comedy is a solo spoken performance, usually comic, built on direct address to the crowd. It can be a club act, a stage show or a recorded special.

sections.heading: Media reach
sections.text: Radio, television and film are mass media: they send one performance to many people. They carry stage work to audiences who cannot attend. A radio drama uses voice, sound effects and silence; television and film add pictures and editing. They widen reach but change the experience: the audience is no longer in the same room as the performers. Recordings can also preserve performances and create new income, though rights and fees must be agreed.

sections.heading: Audience and marketing
sections.text: Audience research collects evidence about who attends, why, and what they think. Methods include ticket records, surveys, focus groups and watching how people respond. Marketing uses that evidence to choose the message, price, venue and channels such as posters, radio, social media and community groups. A clear title, image and time matter more than vague praise.

sections.heading: Economics of a house
sections.text: The economics of a house compares income from tickets with costs. Fixed costs do not change with audience size, such as hall rent. Variable costs rise with each ticket or performance. Break-even is the audience at which income equals costs. Example: a hall holds 300; tickets cost ₦2,000; fixed costs are ₦480,000; variable cost is ₦200 per ticket. Each ticket gives ₦1,800. Break-even is ₦480,000 ÷ ₦1,800 = 267 tickets. Selling 300 gives profit 300 × ₦1,800 − ₦480,000 = ₦60,000.

keyPoints: Popular theatre aims at a broad audience and often uses music, comedy and familiar stories.
Commercial theatre is run to make money, so cost control and ticket sales matter.
Nigerian travelling theatre toured towns with mixed music, dance and drama.
Radio, television and film widen reach but remove the shared room of live performance.
Audience research uses ticket data, surveys, focus groups and observation to guide marketing.
Break-even tickets = fixed costs ÷ (ticket price − variable cost per ticket), and profit = tickets sold × (ticket price − variable cost per ticket) − fixed costs.

en.title: Playwriting and Dramatic Writing
en.short: Premise, scene and act building, dialogue, rewriting, script format and routes to production.

sections.heading: Premise and character
sections.text:
A premise is one sentence that names the central conflict and what is at stake. It is not a theme, which is the idea the play explores.

Start with a character who wants something urgently and faces a cost. An invented example: a trader in Kano hides her son’s debt, and the lie forces her to choose between the shop and her daughter’s school fees. That sentence gives a subject, a pressure and a possible ending. Test it by asking what happens if the character does nothing. If the answer is 'nothing much', the premise is weak.

sections.heading: Scenes and acts
sections.text:
A scene is a unit of change. A character enters wanting something, meets an obstacle, and leaves in a different position. That change is the turn.

Group scenes into acts; an act ends at a major reversal or decision that makes the next act necessary. In the invented example, a scene where the trader refuses a loan turns when the creditor arrives at the shop. The refusal is no longer possible. Keep each scene tied to the premise.

sections.heading: Dialogue and subtext
sections.text:
Believable dialogue follows what each character wants, knows and would actually say. Cut greetings and explanations that only inform the audience. Subtext is the meaning under the words.

An invented exchange: 'Mama, the school sent a letter.' 'Put it on the table.' The fear of the fee is subtext. Read lines aloud; if they are hard to say, rewrite them. Let characters interrupt, dodge and lie.

sections.heading: Rewriting and format
sections.text:
Rewriting is where a play is made. A table read, with actors sitting and reading, shows what is unclear. A staged reading adds an audience and some movement. Listen for confusion, not praise. Revise, then repeat.

Format a script plainly: character names in capitals, dialogue beneath, stage directions in brackets, a title page and page numbers. Routes to production and publication include theatre companies, festivals, competitions, workshops and drama publishers; guidelines differ by country, so check current submission rules.

keyPoints: A premise names the central conflict and what is at stake in one sentence.
A scene turns when a character’s attempt meets an obstacle and the situation changes.
Acts group scenes around major reversals or decisions.
Dialogue should follow character want and vocabulary; subtext is meaning under the words.
Rewriting through table reads and staged readings is part of making the play.
Script format and submission guidelines vary by country and publisher; check current rules.

en.title: Theatre Practice in Nigeria and Africa Today: Companies, Festivals and Funding
en.short: The current ecology of theatre in Nigeria and Africa: companies, festivals, universities, screen crossover and funding.

sections.heading: Companies and venues
sections.text:
The ecology of theatre means the network of people, places and money that lets performance happen. A repertory company keeps a stock of plays and performs them in rotation. Some permanent repertory houses exist in Africa, but many companies are project-based: they gather actors for one production and disband.

Venues range from purpose-built theatres to halls, courtyards and converted spaces. A company’s choice of venue shapes its costs, audience and style.

sections.heading: Festivals and universities
sections.text:
Festivals bring companies and audiences together. They range from community and school events to national and international festivals. In Nigeria, the National Festival of Arts and Culture (NAFEST) is a federal government event, hosted by a different state each year; states and local areas also hold their own festivals.

University theatres are teaching venues run by drama or theatre arts departments. They mount seasons, train crews and actors, host visiting companies, and sometimes rent space to outside groups. Their budgets come through the university. Suppose a troupe in Ibadan stages a play at a university theatre, then tours it to a state festival.

sections.heading: Screen crossover
sections.text:
Film and television crossover means that stage workers also work in screen media. In Nigeria, actors, designers and directors move between theatre and Nollywood, the country’s film industry.

This brings income and wider audiences, but it can pull artists away from rehearsal and change schedules. A play may later become a film or web series. Other African countries have their own screen industries.

sections.heading: Funding and organisation
sections.text:
Funding comes from box office, government grants, sponsorships, donations, non-governmental organisations and international cultural bodies. The mix differs by country and year. Some countries have arts councils; others rely on ministries, state governments or private foundations.

Practitioner unions and guilds negotiate fees and conditions, but their names and legal status vary. In Nigeria, for example, the Actors Guild of Nigeria is a known body; other countries have their own. Check current official sources before relying on any rule or fund.

keyPoints: Theatre ecology is the network of companies, venues, festivals, training institutions, media and funders that support performance.
A repertory company keeps plays in rotation, while many African companies work on a project basis.
Festivals and university theatres provide performance platforms, audiences and training.
Film and television crossover, including Nollywood, brings income and audiences but can affect stage schedules.
Funding mixes box office, government, sponsors, donors and cultural bodies, and the mix varies by country and year.
Unions, guilds and funding bodies differ by country, so check current local official sources.

en.title: Theatre Ethics and Professional Practice
en.short: Contracts, fees, credits, copyright, royalties, censorship, duty of care and safe practice.

sections.heading: Contracts and rights
sections.text:
A contract is a legally binding agreement. In theatre it should state the fee, payment dates, rehearsal and performance dates, cancellation, expenses, credits and who owns or licenses the work. Fees vary by country, venue, union agreement and experience, so check current local rates. A royalty is a payment for the right to perform or reproduce a work, often a percentage of ticket income set in a licence. Copyright is national law: economic rights such as performance and adaptation, and moral rights (credit and integrity of the work), differ between countries, so get written permission. Credits are agreed billing in programmes and publicity.

In an invented Lagos example, producer Ada licenses Tunde’s play for three shows at 10% of ticket income. If 600 tickets sell at ₦2,000, gross is 600 × ₦2,000 = ₦1,200,000, and the royalty is 10% × ₦1,200,000 = ₦120,000.

sections.heading: Censorship and care
sections.text: Censorship is control of what may be shown or said. It may come from law, a classification board, a venue licence or self-censorship. Rules differ by country, so check local law and seek advice before a risky production. Duty of care is the legal and ethical duty to avoid foreseeable harm. It covers performers and audiences: risk assessments, consent, safeguarding (protecting children and vulnerable people), harassment policies, accessible venues and clear emergency plans. Content warnings help audiences, but they do not replace legal advice.

sections.heading: Safe practice and codes
sections.text:
Safe practice means planning to prevent injury. Warm up, use a qualified fight director for stage combat, check weapons and props, and choreograph intimacy with consent. Heights, rigging, electrical work and fire effects need trained staff and local rules. Manage crowds, fatigue and mental health, and report incidents.

Codes of conduct differ by country and union. Performers’ unions and guilds, such as Equity in the United Kingdom and Actors’ Equity or SAG-AFTRA in the United States, set rules on hours, breaks, fees and safety. Local guilds and employers may set others. Always check the current code that applies to your production.

keyPoints: A written contract should set fee, dates, cancellation, expenses, credits and rights.
Fees and royalties vary by country, venue and agreement, so check current local rates and the licence.
Copyright is national law; get written permission to perform or adapt a work.
Censorship rules differ by country and may come from law, licensing or venue policy.
Duty of care requires risk assessment, consent, safeguarding and emergency planning for performers and audiences.
Safe practice includes warm-ups, qualified fight direction, checked props, trained rigging and reporting incidents; union codes differ by country.

en.title: Research Methods for Theatre Studies
en.short: Covers research design, literature review, archives, interviews, ethnography, practice enquiry, ethics and writing up.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text: Start with a question that evidence can answer, not a broad topic such as “theatre in Nigeria”. Name a case, period or practice. A literature review maps what scholars already say and shows the gap your project fills. Search databases, journals and books, and record full citation details. Choose methods that fit: archives for history, interviews for people’s accounts, observation for live process, practice for making work. Check time, access and ethics before you begin.

sections.heading: Archives and productions
sections.text: Archival research uses primary sources such as programmes, prompt books, photographs, reviews and recordings. Find them through catalogues and archive guides, ask archivists for permission, and note box and folder numbers. Production research studies how a show was made and received. Keep a research journal, rehearsal notes and publicity. Cite a recorded performance by title, director, company, venue and date. A programme note is not neutral fact; ask who wrote it and why.

sections.heading: People and practice
sections.text: Interviews are usually semi-structured: prepare questions but follow useful leads. Record only with consent, transcribe, then code by grouping repeated ideas. Ethnography means observing, and sometimes joining, a theatre community over time; write field notes and reflect on your own effect on the setting. Practice-based research treats the creative work as main evidence, with a written commentary. Practice-led research starts from making and aims at new understanding about practice. Definitions vary, so check your department’s rules.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing up
sections.text: Many institutions require ethics approval before collecting data from people; check your own rule. The committee checks informed consent, anonymity, the right to withdraw and care for vulnerable participants. Get permission for recordings and archive material. Cite consistently in one style, such as Harvard, MLA or Chicago, as your department requires. In a small project or final production portfolio, state the question, explain the method, present evidence, analyse it and reflect critically. Example: a student interviews a director, observes two rehearsals with permission and keeps a journal; the portfolio links these evidence types to the question.

keyPoints: A research question should be specific enough to answer with evidence and should guide your choice of method.
A literature review shows what is already known and where your project adds new understanding.
Archival and production research use primary sources, permissions and careful citation of documents and performances.
Interviews need informed consent, transcription and coding; ethnography adds observation, field notes and reflection on your own effect.
Practice-based research treats the creative work as main evidence, while practice-led research starts from practice to build new understanding; definitions vary.
Get ethics approval before collecting data, and write up the question, method, evidence and critical reflection with consistent citation.

en.title: Advanced Dramatic and Performance Theory
en.short: Semiotics, phenomenology, postdramatic, postcolonial and feminist readings of stage performance.

sections.heading: Stage signs
sections.text: Semiotics studies signs. A sign has a signifier, the physical mark, and a signified, the meaning it carries. Stage signs may be iconic, resembling what they show, indexical, pointing to a cause or presence, or symbolic, meaning by convention. A red cloth can be an icon of blood, an index of sacrifice, or a symbol of danger. Semiotics asks how costumes, gestures, light and space form codes that an audience learns to read. Performance is treated as meaning-making.

sections.heading: Bodies and audiences
sections.text: Phenomenology asks what performance is like as lived experience. It attends to the actor’s body, the spectator’s body and the shared space between them. Reception theory asks how audiences make meaning. A horizon of expectations is the set of assumptions a spectator brings; co-presence is the fact of being in the same room. These approaches ask how a production feels and how spectators complete it, not only what its signs mean.

sections.heading: Postdramatic theatre
sections.text: Hans-Thies Lehmann’s term postdramatic theatre describes work where the dramatic text is no longer the organising centre. Scenography, bodies, sound, media and duration may lead. The spectator is often addressed as a co-present witness rather than a story-follower. The framework asks what happens when plot and character lose their hierarchy. It is not a label for all new theatre, and critics debate its usefulness.

sections.heading: Power and gender
sections.text: Postcolonial reading asks how performance represents colonial history, race, nation and power. It looks for othering, making a group seem foreign, and hybridity, the mixing of cultures. Feminist reading asks how gender, the body, labour and the gaze are staged. The gaze concerns who looks and who is looked at. Take an invented Lagos production, Market Women’s Choir. Semiotics reads cloth and chant as signs; phenomenology reads the audience’s bodily response; postdramatic theory reads its form; postcolonial theory reads colonial history; feminist theory reads gendered labour. Each asks a different question of the same event.

keyPoints: Semiotics reads stage elements as signs within learned codes.
Phenomenology and reception theory ask how performance is lived and completed by spectators.
Postdramatic theatre decentres the dramatic text in favour of scenography, bodies and media.
Postcolonial criticism examines representation, othering, hybridity and power.
