Feminist performance criticism examines gender, the body, labour and the gaze.
Different frameworks answer different questions about the same production, so they can be combined critically.

en.title: Performance Studies: Ritual, Performativity and Everyday Life
en.short: Schechner’s broad spectrum, Turner on ritual and social drama, and performativity from Austin to Butler.

sections.heading: The broad spectrum
sections.text:
Richard Schechner argues that performance is far wider than theatre. He defines performance as restored behaviour: actions that are repeated, rehearsed and cited, so the doer behaves twice, as themselves and as someone else. He arranges a broad spectrum running from ritual, shamanism and play, through games, sport, dance and theatre, to everyday greeting and self-presentation.

Schechner also describes performance as a braid of efficacy, the ritual work of transformation, and entertainment, the pleasure of showing. Every performance mixes the two in some proportion, and the balance shifts with context.

sections.heading: Ritual and social drama
sections.text:
Victor Turner, following Arnold van Gennep, described rites of passage as separation, liminality and reaggregation. Liminality is the threshold stage where normal rules are suspended and communitas, an egalitarian bond among participants, may appear. Turner coined liminoid for optional, leisure-based forms in modern societies.

His social drama has four phases: breach, crisis, redressive action, then reintegration or schism. Take a campus case: a sudden fee increase is the breach, student protest is the crisis, a senate committee is redressive action, and the outcome is settlement or a lasting split.

sections.heading: Performativity
sections.text:
J.L. Austin, in How to Do Things with Words (1962), separated constative utterances, which describe, from performatives, which act, as when a registrar says 'I pronounce you husband and wife'. Performatives depend on felicity conditions: the right person, circumstances and intention. Judith Butler (Gender Trouble, 1990) extended this: gender is performative, made real by repeated citation of norms, not a costume an actor freely chooses.

To read a non-theatrical event as performance, ask who frames it, who watches, what behaviour is repeated, and what the event accomplishes.

keyPoints: Schechner defines performance as restored behaviour: actions repeated and cited rather than invented fresh.
His broad spectrum places ritual, play, sport, theatre and everyday life on one continuum.
Turner’s liminality names the threshold stage of ritual, where communitas, an egalitarian bond, may arise.
Turner’s social drama moves through breach, crisis, redressive action and reintegration or schism.
Austin’s performatives do things rather than describe them, and depend on felicity conditions.
Butler’s performativity treats identity as produced by repeated citation of norms, not free choice.

en.title: Dissertation Methods in Theatre Research
en.short: Narrowing a question, theory, archival, ethnographic and practice-based methods, chapters, ethics and publication.

sections.heading: Narrowing and framing
sections.text:
A dissertation question must be answerable with your time and access. Start broad, then limit by place, period, group, text or practice. An invented example: a student interested in community theatre narrows to how one youth troupe in Kano uses forum theatre with market traders. Forum theatre, after Augusto Boal, invites spectators to intervene in a scene.

A theoretical frame is the set of concepts that shapes analysis. It is not a list of theorists. Choose two or three ideas, define them, and show how they guide your questions. The literature review should identify a gap, not just summarise.

sections.heading: Choosing methods
sections.text: Archival research uses documents such as programmes, reviews, letters and records. It needs a source list, dates and attention to missing evidence. Ethnographic research uses participant observation, interviews and fieldnotes to understand a theatre community. It requires informed consent, reflexivity (examining your own effect on the field) and careful notes. Practice-based research treats creative work as part of the inquiry. You make a performance or design, document it, reflect on it, and submit a written exegesis that explains the claim. Methods can be combined.

sections.heading: Structure and supervision
sections.text: A common structure is introduction, literature review and theory, methodology, analysis and conclusion. Practice-based theses add a portfolio or performance and an exegesis. Agree a schedule with your supervisor, send written agendas before meetings, and record decisions. Supervision is guidance, not proofreading. Ethics approval is usually required before fieldwork. Address informed consent, anonymity, vulnerable participants, permissions and copyright. Use one referencing style consistently, keep full records, and never present another person’s words or ideas as your own.

sections.heading: Publication and conferences
sections.text: A conference paper is a short version of one argument. A journal article needs a contribution and fit with the journal’s scope. Read the call for papers and author guidelines. Discuss authorship with your supervisor and collaborators. Expect peer review: other scholars assess your work. Revise and keep a note of changes. Do not send the paper to two journals at once.

keyPoints: Narrow the question by place, period, group, text or practice so it is answerable.
A theoretical frame defines the concepts that guide analysis; it is not a list of theorists.
Archival, ethnographic and practice-based methods suit different questions and can be combined.
Practice-based research submits creative work plus an exegesis explaining the claim.
Agree a schedule with your supervisor, keep records, and settle ethics before fieldwork.
Use one referencing style consistently and follow the venue’s rules for conferences and journals.

en.title: Intercultural and Applied Theatre at the Frontier
en.short: Intercultural performance, adapting classics into African forms, applied theatre, ownership debates and digital performance.

sections.heading: Intercultural performance
sections.text:
Intercultural theatre deliberately combines forms, training or texts from different cultures. Cross-cultural study compares traditions; intercultural practice expects them to change each other. Peter Brook staged the Mahabharata with an international cast in 1985, Ariane Mnouchkine’s Théâtre du Soleil drew on Indian and Japanese forms, and Eugenio Barba’s theatre anthropology compared performer training across forms such as kathakali.

Patrice Pavis modelled the exchange as an hourglass: a source culture is filtered through the director’s staging before a target audience receives it. Rustom Bharucha attacked such work as cultural tourism that takes fragments without the beliefs and labour that give them meaning.

sections.heading: Adapting classics
sections.text: Adaptation is not translation; it moves a classic’s conflict into a new social world. Ola Rotimi’s The Gods Are Not to Blame resets Oedipus in a Yoruba kingdom. Femi Osofisan’s Women of Owu takes Euripides’ Trojan Women to the aftermath of an inter-Yoruba war. Wole Soyinka’s Bacchae (1973) reads the play as a communion rite. In South Africa, Fugard, Kani and Ntshona’s The Island (1973) staged Antigone inside a prison cell.

sections.heading: Applied theatre
sections.text: Applied theatre is theatre made with a specific group, outside commercial venues, for a stated purpose. Augusto Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed, especially Forum Theatre, lets spectators stop a scene and test other actions; they become spect-actors. Health projects dramatise prevention and stigma, justice projects work in prisons and with victims, conflict projects build dialogue between divided groups. Helen Nicholson and James Thompson stress the facilitator’s duties: informed consent, confidentiality, and not mining participants’ pain for an audience.

sections.heading: Ownership and the digital
sections.text: Debate turns on ownership. Does a director need consent from a source community? Defenders of borrowing cite artistic freedom and long histories of exchange; critics cite power, colonial history and misrepresentation. Digital performance adds questions: who owns a recording, and what liveness means when audiences are remote. Steve Dixon’s Digital Performance (2007) surveys the field, and companies such as Blast Theory work across games, phones and physical space.

keyPoints: Intercultural theatre combines forms from different cultures; cross-cultural study mainly compares them.
Pavis’s hourglass model shows a source culture filtered through staging before a target audience receives it.
Bharucha argues that intercultural borrowing can become cultural tourism that ignores a form’s beliefs and labour.
Adapting a classic relocates its conflict, as in Rotimi’s Oedipus and Osofisan’s Women of Owu.
Applied theatre is made with a group for a stated purpose, and Boal’s Forum Theatre turns spectators into spect-actors.
Facilitators need informed consent and confidentiality, and should not mine participants’ stories.
